faq: Do you change anything during the audit?
No. An audit is read-only. You get a report and decide what to act on. If you want us to fix items, we quote that as a separate order in writing.
What do you need to run the audit?
The source code or the store link, plus read access to your store dashboard if you want listing data reviewed. We never need your password and only ask for view access.
Will the audit find every possible bug?
It covers the areas listed and highlights the most important risks, but no review can find everything. We state clearly what we checked and what we did not.
Can you check against store policy changes?
Yes. We compare your extension with the current Chrome Web Store program policies and flag risks such as broad permissions, unclear data use or missing disclosures.

desc:
A browser extension code and store audit from Ecom Swift LLC is a written review of your extension's code, permissions and store listing, with every finding ranked so you know what to fix first and why it matters.

## What is a browser extension audit?

A browser extension audit is an independent review that checks how your extension is built, how it behaves in the browser and how it appears in the store. The result is a report, not a code change. You learn where the risks are before a user complaint, a slow startup or a store warning teaches you the hard way.

Extensions are small programs with large access. They can read pages, store data and run in the background, so small mistakes show up quickly in reviews and in store policy emails. An outside review catches what the person who wrote the code no longer sees.

## Why a ranked report beats a long list of notes

Most reviews fail because they list fifty items with equal weight. You cannot act on that. We rank each finding by importance, so a leaked key or an over-broad permission sits above a spacing complaint.

Every point in the report answers three questions: what is wrong, why it matters and how to fix it. That means your own developer, a freelancer or our team can pick up the list and start work the same day. It also gives you something concrete to show a partner or investor who asks whether the extension is in good shape.

## What a thorough extension audit covers

- Permissions and host access, checked against what each feature really needs.
- Manifest V3 readiness: service worker behavior, remote code rules and request handling.
- Message passing between popup, background worker and content scripts.
- Storage use, including what is saved, where and for how long.
- Startup time, memory use and work done on every page load.
- Security habits such as handling of keys, user input and calls to outside servers.
- Store listing accuracy: title, description, screenshots and privacy answers.
- Policy risks, such as unclear data use or features the listing does not mention.
- Onboarding and first-run screens, where users often give up.
- Error handling, so failures show a useful message instead of a silent break.

## How we run the audit

We start by reading the manifest, because it shows what the extension asks the browser to allow. Then we load the extension in Chrome and Edge, use each feature as a new user would and watch the console, the network calls and the memory it uses. We compare what the code does with what your store listing and privacy answers say, since mismatches are a common cause of warnings.

The Basic, Standard and Premium packages differ in depth. Basic focuses on code and permissions. Standard adds the listing review, a performance check and a call to walk through the results. Premium goes further into user flow, data use and a fix roadmap, and includes a re-check once you have acted on the top items.

We do not change your code or your store page during the audit. If you want help with the fixes, that can be added afterward.

## Do and avoid when you receive an audit

**Do:**
- Fix the top-ranked findings before the minor ones.
- Share the report with whoever maintains the code.
- Ask questions on the call while the details are fresh.
- Re-test in a clean browser profile after every fix.
- Keep the report so you can compare against the next release.

**Avoid:**
- Treating a clean report as permission to stop checking after future browser updates.
- Removing a permission without testing the feature that used it.
- Rewriting the whole extension when a handful of fixes would do.
- Hiding known issues from the reviewer, since that only weakens the findings.
- Ignoring the store listing section because it is not code.

## Who benefits most

This service suits a founder who bought or inherited an extension and wants to know what they own. It also suits a developer who is preparing a major release and wants a second pair of eyes before reviewers see it. And it suits a team that received a store warning or a wave of one-star feedback about speed and wants to find the cause.

## What we need from you

Send the source code as a zip file or a repository invite, or a link to the store listing if the code is hard to share. Tell us what worries you most and who your users are. A short note about past store warnings helps a great deal.

We never need your passwords. If you want us to look at the developer dashboard, add us with the access level your store account offers, or send screenshots of the relevant pages instead. We confirm what we received and then work through the review in order.
